title: Classical MIS Dichotomy Conjecture
statement_text: For every connected graph $H$, Maximum Independent Set in $H$-free graphs is in $\mathsf{P}$ if and only if $H \in \{P_\ell\}_{\ell} \cup \{S_{i,j,k}\}_{i \leq j \leq k}$.
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. Alekseev observed that subdividing each edge $2t$ times increases the independence number by exactly $t|E(G)|$, so MIS stays NP-hard on graphs that locally look like paths or subdivided claws; hence if a connected $H$ is neither a path nor a subdivided claw, MIS is NP-complete on $H$-free graphs. The conjecture asserts the converse. Known polynomial cases include $P_4$-free graphs (cographs), $P_5$-free (Lokshtanov, Vatshelle, Villanger) and $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik et al.), claw-free and fork-free ($S_{1,1,2}$-free) graphs. The complexity is open for $P_7$-, $S_{1,1,3}$- and $S_{1,2,2}$-free graphs, and there is no triple $i\le j\le k$ for which MIS is known to be NP-hard on $S_{i,j,k}$-free graphs. A stronger conjecture was proposed by Lozin.

title: Parameterized MIS Dichotomy
statement_text: For each connected graph $H$, is MIS (randomized) FPT or $W[1]$-hard in $H$-free graphs, parameterized by the size $k$ of the solution?
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. FPT means solvable in time $f(k)n^{O(1)}$, and $W[1]$-hardness is the standard evidence against FPT; MIS is $W[1]$-hard in general graphs. This is the parameterized counterpart of the classical P versus NP-complete dichotomy for MIS in $H$-free graphs, and may be even harder. No FPT algorithm is known for the classical open cases ($P_7$-, $S_{1,1,3}$- and $S_{1,2,2}$-free graphs), and Alekseev's NP-hardness reduction does not show $W[1]$-hardness, so a priori more graphs $H$ are candidates; for instance MIS is FPT on $K_t$-free graphs by Ramsey's theorem. Dabrowski et al. initiated the systematic study and showed FPT for all four-vertex $H$ except $C_4$. Bonnet et al. gave parameterized analogues of Alekseev's reduction, leaving as connected candidates for FPT roughly the paths and subdivided claws whose vertices are blown up into cliques. This paper settles all five-vertex graphs $H$: the four remaining five-vertex cases (including the dart and the cricket) are randomized FPT.

title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: For any integer $t$, MIS can be solved in FPT time in $P(t,t,t,t)$-free graphs.
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. FPT means solvable in time $f(k)n^{O(1)}$, and $W[1]$-hardness is the standard evidence against FPT; MIS is $W[1]$-hard in general graphs. $P(t_1,\dots,t_\ell)$ denotes the graph obtained from the path $v_1\dots v_\ell$ by substituting a clique of size $t_i$ for each $v_i$ (vertices of consecutive cliques are all adjacent), and $P_\ell(t)=P(t,\dots,t)$ with $\ell$ entries. MIS was shown FPT on $P(t,t,t)$-free graphs by Bonnet et al.; this conjecture is the natural next step for clique-substituted four-vertex paths. As partial progress the authors prove that for every fixed $t\ge1$, MIS is FPT in $P(1,t,t,t)$-free graphs, where one end of the path is not blown up, using FPT Turing-reductions on variants of cographs with parameterized noise.

title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For any integers $t$ and $\ell$, MIS is FPT in $P_\ell(t)$-free graphs, where $P_\ell(t) = P(t, t, \ldots, t)$ with the sequence $t, t, \ldots, t$ of length $\ell$.
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. FPT means solvable in time $f(k)n^{O(1)}$, and $W[1]$-hardness is the standard evidence against FPT; MIS is $W[1]$-hard in general graphs. $P(t_1,\dots,t_\ell)$ denotes the graph obtained from the path $v_1\dots v_\ell$ by substituting a clique of size $t_i$ for each $v_i$ (vertices of consecutive cliques are all adjacent), and $P_\ell(t)=P(t,\dots,t)$ with $\ell$ entries. This is described as a far more distant milestone than the four-vertex case ($P(t,t,t,t)$-free graphs, conjectured FPT; the authors prove FPT for $P(1,t,t,t)$-free graphs, and FPT was known for $P(t,t,t)$-free graphs). The case $t=1$ already contains $P_\ell$-free graphs: the parameterized complexity of MIS is open in $P_7$-free graphs, and no easy FPT algorithm is known even on $P_5$-free graphs.

title: Informal belief on FPT candidates
statement_text: There will be very few connected candidates $H$ (connected graphs $H$ for which known reductions do not show MIS to be $W[1]$-hard on $H$-free graphs) for which MIS in $H$-free graphs will not end up in (randomized) FPT.
context_text: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) asks for a largest set of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (in the parameterized version, whether there is one of size $k$, with parameter $k$). A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. $P_\ell$ is the path on $\ell$ vertices, and $S_{i,j,k}$ is the subdivided claw: the tree with exactly one vertex of degree three from which start three paths with $i$, $j$ and $k$ edges. FPT means solvable in time $f(k)n^{O(1)}$, and $W[1]$-hardness is the standard evidence against FPT; MIS is $W[1]$-hard in general graphs. Bonnet et al. gave parameterized analogues of Alekseev's NP-hardness reduction, which show $W[1]$-hardness unless $H$ has a restricted form. According to the paper, the connected FPT candidates must be chordal, have no induced $K_{1,4}$ and no induced tree with two vertices of degree at least three. They must also fit either a path whose vertices are blown up into cliques (consecutive cliques joined by complete bipartite graphs minus at most one edge, with at most one junction instead a $2K_2$-free bipartite graph), or both a subdivided claw and the line graph of a subdivided claw with blown-up vertices, plus further technical restrictions. Some graphs outside these forms (for instance $T(1,2,2)$) are $W[1]$-hard, showing how delicate the dichotomy is. As first evidence for their belief, the authors show that the four remaining five-vertex candidates among the 34 graphs on five vertices all give (randomized) FPT algorithms.
